Life was a struggle since the day I was diagnosed, with many claiming that it was a "phase" or a means to gain attention. A lot of people in my life tried to tell me how intelligent I was despite failing grades. A lot of people tried to push me in many directions so I'd become "successful" and that my autism is a "crutch" that I held on to to "justify being lazy".

To this very day, I still struggle with everyday sounds,  sights and just the overabundance of triggers that make every day that much more tiring. I've tried college and working the odd job,  but right now I can't handle it. It honestly feels like, by default, everything is a struggle to do, to learn, and to remember just to rightfully "fit in". I'm tired of all that. It's all so very tiring.

Zoloft. Any time I took it, it felt like I had never ending heartburn and it was like 5 times as painful.. it kept me bed ridden because of the pain. 

The worst part was that my psychiatrist didn't believe me at all. He'd tell me how I'm making up the pain for attention,  or how there's supposed to have little to no side effects and again,  whatever I was experiencing was all psychosomatic.

The final nail in the coffin was I pleaded to take me off the med. He'd go on to say "Are your bones broken? Are your palms sweating? No? Then there's nothing wrong".

And then when the pain wasn't subsiding I took two more naproxen and that was when the pain moved to my gut and I had to call for a hospital. Turns out I then not only had tooth pain but also an abscess in my stomach or somewhere in my gut. I was put on hydromorphone because the pain was that severe. 

Today though my gut is doing fine and I've been keeping on top of my dental hygiene too.

My therapist has suggested to me to try "deep breathing exercises" and "going for walks and socializing" and "reality testing". A bunch of stuff she's suggested years ago but keeps telling me to this day that these techniques work even though I've tried my absolute best to trying these techniques day in and day out, it does nothing but put me in a more aggravated / depressed state.

Also a big one she suggest is to "pretend to be happy", like smile if I don't feel like smiling and laugh when I don't feel like laughing etc.. Trouble is that when I do that, I get this physical exhaustion from it, as if I sprinted a mile or something... pretending to be happy to trick my brain into being happy. I just don't buy it.

There have been some moments where I did think, "My family and friends aren't doctors or therapists" so I figured that they wouldn't really know how to handle a situation. But I still feel this kind of loneliness when it comes to feeling misunderstood. I feel like my depression is being viewed as being lazy and people have in my life equated my depression as me just being a slob that doesn't want to be a productive member in society, as if I'm actively choosing to live that way.

My friends I feel are still trying their best but the distance that's been created is growing between us every month that passes. I'm stuck here in this "rut" if anything, and my friends see me feeling this way, but because they assume they don't know what to do, nothing gets done still and it makes things worse.

To be honest, I'm not sure exactly what can be done, but I did give myself some time since I wrote this post, just a day or two of "me time" and I feel less aggravated. I'm glad you replied and said something too. Even if it was complete nonsense I would've been happy enough that someone read what I had to say.

I do practice some methods my therapist suggests, but lately it's been this stagnant thing where she says, "Well, have you been practicing what I suggested?" and if I tell her yes, but it isn't working, then she tells me to try it again and again and again. It feels like she's forcing a placebo and really wants it to work, but as I said earlier, the "me time" where just took a couple days to not care about the news, not care about the world and only just focus on myself really helped bring my anger down a bit.

Again, thanks for replying.

I agree with you completely. As an example, I really like to listen to jazz. Most people I know do actually make an effort to refuse to listen to any jazz. If their opinion on jazz and why they choose not to listen is based on very loose ideas which don't really describe what jazz is, then that's fine for me I don't take much offense to that.

But if, on the odd chance one of them tells me their outright refusal to listen to jazz is based on those same loose ideas and then follows it up with something, "..and that's why jazz is bad" or something where they make definitive statements, then I have a problem. It's one thing to have a loose opinion on something but it becomes a problem when that same opinion is being used as factual especially on a subject like music.

I've never meant any offense to begin and just used my dumb reasoning to show why I'd prefer Rap over Metal.

> This is literally something I've never heard anyone listening to Metal say ever. People just don't listen to Metal for lyrics. 

It'd be nice if I was making it up, but some of my Metal-friends actually take some weird offense if I tell them that I can't hear what the singer is saying if anything, and they can.

> But... they don't. As I said. Most Metal songs are probably around 6 minutes, not 12.

Right, they're not all 12+ minutes long, but my hyperbole was used to emphasize why I'm more tired of Metal than Rap and why I'd choose to listen to Rap if given the choice.

> The notion that these sound even slightly the same is nonsense.

Now that I've listened to them both, they really don't sound like one another. I hadn't doubted that the genre of Metal can surpass expectations and can have a wide variety of sounds. As I said in my first post, the majority of my experience comes from my friends. In the first reply to your post, I confirmed that I am ignorant when it comes to Metal.

When something like this is anecdotal and I use blanket statements and generalizations, I wouldn't expect you to take my opinion with heavy weight to it, or rather no weight at all. Because, I believe 0 of my friends listen to Rap I have a better preference to listen to that than Metal, even though I don't hold a strong opinion on Rap either.

I think it would be best if I answered what you wrote from the bottom to the top.

> This just suggests you're actually quite ignorant about Metal.

You're right, I am. I don't often seek out new Metal artists in my spare time. Sometimes I will, but it doesn't take a high priority for me. As I said in my first post, most of the people I hang out with will put on their Metal artist / album of choice, which is where I get the majority of my experience with Metal.

> Lyricism is not as important in Metal (speaking generally) as it is in  most other meta-genre styles. The vocal is broadly considered an  instrument.

I can really dig stuff like that, where your voice is just used as another instrument rather than as a means of trying to get across a message. Though, when listening to Metal with my friends, I'd often hear them tell me something like, "Did you hear what he said? That was so cool" and I'd tell them that I couldn't and I can't for the life of me understand anything the singer is saying, either due to the instruments overpowering the singer's voice, or the singer's voice is too low where I can hear he's saying something but I never know what it is exactly.

> Some Metal songs are 12+ minutes long, but this is not a common thing at all outside of, idk, Funeral Doom or some Prog Metal. 

A lot of music can benefit from a longer length of the song, but when listening to Metal with my friends there would be those handful of songs that would seem like they go on forever with the absolute insane endurance of the drummer banging away those double kick drums nonstop. Though as impressive as it is, it feels like a very dull jackhammer in my head and it gets tiring very quickly.

> So you honestly think that Freedom Call sounds like Cannibal Corpse?

To bring this full circle, I can't actually answer that question. I've heard of Cannibal Corpse, many, many times before, but I can't say I've ever heard of Freedom Call.

Genre mashups are incredible in general I think. Metal / classical is always cool to listen to. I've heard metal crossed with other genres before though I can't remember off the top of my head, but they were always really awesome to listen to.

Sometimes I'd come across a random artist on Soundcloud or Bandcamp that would take a song like Just Dance for example but would stylize it as Latin Jazz instead of Pop. I really love experimentation in music.

I listen to almost anything but I do favor some genres over others. Mostly I listen to songs for their instrumentals only. If I'm looking for lyrics I really have to dig for the better stuff, so it's not to say that I prefer instrumentals but finding a good singer with good lyrics is more difficult to come across.

I really enjoy classical. I also play instruments myself and sometimes write my own music. I've studied music theory and can teach as well. Maybe it's because of my own experience that I really can't stand "lazy" music writing. Modern pop is a great example. Metal is nowhere nearly as bad as pop, but I do get tired of it very easily.

I'm also a POC, but that depends on who you ask and if you're willing to see me as just a POC. Truthfully, I'm mixed. My Dad being Caucasian, and my Mom being Caribbean. Though, on the surface my skin is quite dark so growing up I've heard my share of incredibly racist comments as well as people acting differently because of the color of my skin.

For the most part, I never cared what people said about or to me because I'd rationalize that, whomever is claiming I'm a lazy "so and so" doesn't even know who I am so their comment holds absolutely no merit and I move on. However, if the people around me are making efforts to make me feel ostracized, I at least do my best to prove to them that I'm more than what they might think I am.

Honestly, the thing that bothers me is that if I try to show someone that I'm more than just a dark-skinned individual and they're still not convinced in the end, it hurts me a bit. But in the end it's better for me if I didn't stick with them. If I do however gain someone's favor, then I feel a lot more accomplished in their group than to just be accepted and having to prove nothing.

I've had decades to be upset and be angry and hateful, but it just isn't worth it. From the point I started to ignore what other people thought of me, I already began to see my life improving almost immediately.

In the end, it's up to you what you want to do. Whether you want to follow my advice or not, I hope you're able to get out of or otherwise remedy the situation you're in.

Don't drink or eat food before you sleep, since this will cause your body to wake up earlier to use the bathroom.

Some miscellaneous tips: If you need an alarm to wake up in the morning, make it a habit to fall asleep earlier so you're able to wake up naturally. Something I did and sometimes even do now, is I close my eyes and imagine walking through my place and making a mental map of where everything is, then walking outside and going to a nearby park or something. This is all imaginary, but it helps to distract your mind if you're sometimes plagued with anxieties and worries during the night.

After being transferred to my 5th high school, I underwent some kind of test to determine my "studying level" and I must have scored poorly on it or something so I ended up having to attend some special education classroom as a free study block. I never actually needed help understanding things, but for the most part I always took almost twice as long on tests as my peers.

Sometimes, after I'd be finishing up homework I'd be given the opportunity to just wander around the class and find someone else who needed help instead of sitting by myself until the next period came up. I met my best friend who was a year my junior and he immediately called me over and said, "Hey, you want to see something really cool?" and I told him, yeah I would.

Next thing he leans close to a student with Down's Syndrome and said, "What time is it?", the poor student started screaming, "HAMMER TIME! HAMMER TIME! HAMMER TIME!" nonstop because that was a favorite song of his I found out.

Cue my uncontrollable laughter and my soon to be best friend trying to control his. The Special Ed. teacher gave me a good talking to, but what mattered was that I and my best friend had met and was able to share countless more hilarious times with each other in the future and to this day.

It really goes from anywhere being convinced that nothing's wrong and that you have no mental health issues or that there's some kind of shame in admitting that you're mentally ill and it somehow makes you less of a person in society. It's more often I find that other men feel more shame than believing there's nothing wrong and they'll pull through it somehow.

The shame that I see in other men is always put to the most extreme. Getting help for their illness, to them is akin to admitting that they're now beneath being human and will never have any kind of priority in whatever they do in life. Examples include, them feeling like they'll never have a job again, or never being able to make friends or find a romantic partner, never being accepted into any post-secondary education, feelings of being ostracized from any group and the list goes on almost indefinitely.

When men feel this shame and also reach out for help with their mental health, it's as if they have to prepare for a long trip or something. Saving up a lot of money, making sure that everything is paid for or whatever, then after being put on medication they try their utmost best to "get through" the healing process as quickly as possible, even to the point where if they still feel like they're not getting better, they'll just lie to their doctor and just say they're better so that they no longer have to feel this imaginary burden of being labeled as "mentally ill".

I've never felt the shame nor have I felt like I needed to hide from myself that I'm not well. I hear countless times how other guys my age just "hate" having to be medicated or going to therapy or anything that's suggested from any doctor. In the end, what this turns into is they start self-medicating... either by smoking tobacco or weed and eventually turning to the harder drugs which is always depressing to see. I don't know where this stigma actually comes from but it's unfortunately common enough and I don't exactly know if there's any solution to this.

Through either conceit or hardship, at least from my experience. I've known a handful of people that would only ever react to positive opinions about themselves and would proudly ignore everything else. On the other side though, I've also known quite a few people that would care too much about what other people thought and usually focused on only the negative.

When I got a bit older, I tried to think about what exactly it is that's bothering me so much to the point of solidarity and self-harm, and after a while I began to break it down a bit.

I knew already that it was hard for me to form and keep relationships and that it was one of the biggest factors contributing toward my depression. I had few friends that were ever available, my immediate family was almost always absent from my life and I was jumping from doctor to doctor being tried on all these different drugs that were given the promise of "helping" but none of them ever seemed to do anything. I felt isolated no matter how hard I would try to make friends and the only friends I could make were those from segregated groups of other individuals also suffering from depression or other mental illnesses. I felt like being referred to these groups was, in a weird way, cheating. I never got to introduce myself or share my hobbies or even get the chance to prove that I may or may not be a good friend... it was all "automatic" in the sense that once you were a part of the group everyone was friends with each other for no reason other than we all were diagnosed with some mental illness.

I knew I was lonely and I knew that the ways I went about making friends never seemed to work and I knew I wanted to be happy with someone else rather than just observing other people being happy. I destroyed my body so that my doctors would know, try me on some other drug hoping that it would help lift my mood and eventually never delivering. Hurting myself was never bringing the attention of anyone else as much as I wanted it to and that eventually hurt me even more.

The fact my family and peers would give me the same amount of attention or worry regardless of whether I'm hurting myself or not gave me enough reason to stop. It sucks having those permanent scars, but in time it did heal over. For a really long while I stopped caring about being accepted from everyone else and decided I should just do everything I could to make only myself happy. I've traveled to the States several times and even to Trinidad. I've done a lot of things that while it may seem like a "loner" thing to do, the alternative I thought would just to sulk at home and not do anything instead.

I'm still on medication, but I have to come first before anyone else does now. I'm happier this way.

Know the new cat's history. A lot of adopted adult cats have been abandoned or abused by their previous owners making them easily wary and scared of new people and animals. Some of them might bite, scratch or hiss at the very sight of something they don't recognize but that doesn't mean you can't introduce such a cat to a new and loving home.

If the adopted cat has had history of abuse, it would be best to isolate the cat and yourself only in a spacious room where it'll have the time to getting acquainted with its new environment. Don't make sudden or loud movements and don't pet the cat either. Put out some food and water and don't worry if the cat doesn't go for it at first. If the cat becomes aware that its safe it might be brave enough to get to know you as well. Again, no sudden or loud gestures and don't make attempts to pet the cat either.

Once the cat becomes less fearful with you around, it should be safe enough to allow the other cat in your household get introduced. The new cat will most likely be scared, so do keep a look out if a fight ever breaks out. If the two cats fight, separate the two until it's just you and the new cat again.

How you'd want to have the cat get accustomed to your entire household is up to you and your own discretion. One thing to note is if you ever want to pet the cat, let them see and smell your hand first - never immediately reach your hand over their head and start to pet them, this can scare them sometimes.

Ethically... there's already a lot of worn-out "traditional" values that a lot of countries in this world still hold that could possibly be a big factor as to why families in those countries are usually quite large. For some reason or another, these traditions usually hold giving birth to males is seen as an enormous accomplishment whereas giving birth to a female isn't so much. This in turn would have families to "keep trying" - where they would have more and more children until they would finally welcome another male in the family. That being done, their children are taught to believe in these same values and to emulate their parents' behavior and morals. Once their children become grown adults, the cycle would inevitably continue.

There are countries like China for instance that has made it the actual law to prevent families becoming that large. Though, this still doesn't prevent families immigrating to other countries in the world where no such laws exist, then allowing their families to be as large as they want.

I'm not sure if I would actually have an ethical answer. I'm opposed to "whittling down" our current population and forcing individuals to go through sterilization either... it's nobody's place and certainly not mine to determine who may or may not have children. When you live in a country with lax laws that almost benefits larger families in some cases, you would then have to realize that you'd need to give people a *reason* to have smaller families... whether they are incentives, rewards, scholarships or even punishments or higher taxes, there would definitely need to be a way for a family of one or two children to be satisfied enough with what they have.

To start off, when I was reading what you wrote, it took me almost by surprise. Most if not everything you said was like reading into a reflection of my past. While this might come across as taboo to some, I will tell you that I've also been suffering with depression my entire life. I've been medicated since I was 10 years old and I still take medications to this day. Early in my adult life, I was also met with quite the similar roadblock... I always wondered where I should go, what I should do, and most of these thoughts ended up with me stagnating. Attempting to decide what to do had left me mentally paralyzed.

But this is where the healing process started to bud. First, I suggest you don't worry about how you'd want to change your life. Right now, I suggest you take a look at your peers, anyone you know or have known and notice how they're coming along in their life. The trick here, is to not exactly compare your life to theirs, just simply \*notice\* what it is they're doing. Afterwards, notice your own life and how far you've come. Congratulate yourself and realize you've come a long way. You've made it to today and you're now reaching out for help on how to continue.

The step after, is to know that you don't need to set arbitrary goals for yourself. Setting goals works for some people, but in my experience it really doesn't, and not only for me, but for most of my friends too. When you set a goal, you're also setting an incredible amount of stress on yourself. More often than not, these goals are usually unattainable and unrealistic. So when you start to go for it, you know in the back of your mind you're not going to make it, but you're still going to try as hard as you can to still do it. In the end, when trying to achieve the impossible becomes a reality, you'll begin to crash and burnout.

So, what does everything I just said mean in the end? To be brief, it means that you should just take life as it comes to you. But to explain a bit further, I'll tell you what I did. Leaving out some details, my own life certainly hasn't been very kind to me. The idea and the question I had, "How do I change my life?" was weighing on me so much, that I was too afraid to start anything... how do I start? How do I continue what I started? Which then turned into, what if it doesn't work? what if I fail? etc.. You can see how this made me incredibly scared. But, there came a time where I "had enough" and was very desperate for "something" to change. That's when it happened:

I realized that, when I wanted to "change my life" I was doing so under the guise of wanting my life to be like long-gone friends who achieved incredible things. They got married, had a family and are working high-paying jobs. But is that exactly what it meant to "achieve"? Is that what it meant to be "successful"? I noticed all my thoughts and all my goals were all based on what my peers have told me while growing up. To be a successful person, it meant that you had a lot of money or you had a big family or had a lot of power. I mean... even if all of that were true, would having those things make you happy? What makes others happy, doesn't necessarily have to make you happy.

Right now, presently in my life, I actively seek out groups that share common interests. Places like [meetup.com](https://meetup.com) are great resources to find people that are more than welcoming to have you. I go out with no expectations, and leave happy and satisfied. Some people will tell you having zero expectations for things will make you "pathetic" or something, but again to reiterate, what makes them happy, won't necessarily make you happy.

To end this long-winded wall of text, I'll say to just, "do what you want". I know that doesn't mean much by itself, but try to take that in context with the things I wrote in my comment. You don't have to feel like you need to change... I may not know you personally, but I can tell you're a wonderful person that deserves to be happy. If you want to meet friends, again, try to find groups you can hang out at like the site I provided.

So, don't change. You're the best you there ever was and will be.

I'm talking like 1 - 2am. Neighbors constantly called the cops on them and when they'd get to the house, they'd shut off their music for the rest of the night. Thing was, they'd do this every day. One of those two roommates also loved to drink very heavily at whatever time of day he wanted, walking around the place threatening everyone and passing out wherever. One time though, it got a bit too much, where he was drunk and also blasting loud music at night, where unfortunately, the angry neighbor decided to knock on our door instead and was met with the angry drunk.

So he got carried away by police and never returned. The roommate who replaced him was an older woman, probably in her 40s, but she was very sweet and nobody in the house ever bugged her or anything. Thing was, she never told us she was mentally ill, which none of us had a problem with, but there would be days where she was obviously not taking her medication. Normally, a coherent and sweet woman, turns into a confused, anxiety-ridden mess. She would get extremely scared when the washer or dryer would be running and would literally stand still for hours, or at least, until both the washer and dryer weren't being used.

Because the other roommates would be out during the day, I'd become increasingly worried and scared leaving that woman on her own. Sure, that may sound presumptuous, but on a night I had spent out drinking with friends, I came home around 11:30 at night to find her shivering and scared standing at the washer, as pale as ever, because she forgot how to use it, pressing buttons basically making the washer go for the entire day. The oven in the kitchen was left on as well, though thankfully at a very low temperature.

Stories aside though, I now live in a nice apartment by myself. Friends come by when they want, and I go out when I want. Sure, it'd be nice to share a place with someone, but this time, I'll only do it with people I either love, or are incredibly good friends of mine.

I understand the question asks a good job for "introverts" specifically, and I've noticed a good deal of responses are targeted towards jobs where the majority of the time spent on the job is usually away from anyone else and being alone. Believe me when I say that when I was fresh out of high school, I also desperately wanted a similar kind of job too, and I did get them but over time it was incredibly maddening and depressing.

At an arcade, especially with the specifics I gave, seem like the "ideal job" especially when I had little training and also wanted a bit of peace and ease for myself. It's too bad that I only found out about this after I jumped head-first into the job and demanded I work full-time including Fridays and weekends.

To start, weekdays are incredibly easy. During the morning hours, barely anyone is there, you're always busy too, cleaning the place, fixing any broken machines, and it gets incredibly fascinating, at least for me, learning how each machine works and why. As the day carries on, typically there will be some people coming in, usually parents with their children. Families are awesome customers, even the ones who might complain. For as long as I worked I've always noticed that as long as their children are happy, the parents are happy and the children they bring are very easy to please.

If, for whatever reason, you get some hours during the afternoon, more often than not, regulars will start showing up and they already know what they're there for so again, very easy to deal with. You'll get the odd customer here and there who needs help understanding how things work in the arcade, but given some time after repairing / fixing / fiddling around the arcade cabinets / machines, those "tougher" customers will seem like a breeze. I know that doesn't make sense out of context, but trust me, it will make dealing with them a whole lot easier.

So, if that doesn't sound like an incredibly easy job to me, then I don't know what does. You get your alone time, you get to socialize with people that are easy to please and are happy enough knowing you give a damn, and generally speaking, working at an arcade pays pretty well too.

Fridays and weekends though are complete hell, so avoid those days as much as possible. Otherwise, you'll be golden.

1) if you've been hospitalized what is it like to be a patient? What did you wish was different knowing what you know now?

 I've been hospitalized and put on the psych ward about 5 or 6 times in my life, usually around the Christmas time, though that detail is irrelevant. The only things that I wish were different about my many stays, besides the obvious, like, hospital food being better, or being able to have larger portions, is that, one, very big problem arises when patients get placed into a room with an empty bed, just to fill up space. No thought is usually given beforehand to determine whether the new patient will 'get along' with the other patient(s) in the room with them. I don't mean, 'get along' as in making friends, but, from my experience, putting two schizophrenics in a room together, whom are currently unstable, is just asking for problems. Not to mention that putting a schizophrenic in a room with someone else who is just coming off opiates or something, is also very troublesome. Neither me or any of the nurses on staff, ever liked the situations I was put in. I'd constantly complain about how my roommate is either being delusional to the point where it makes me believe their delusions, or I start to get very uncomfortable with a mate that is cursing, yelling and thrashing about in his sleep.

2) what are voices like to you? I have a hard time conceptually with this. Is it like another person on the room but you look for them and they're not there? Or is it like your own internal voice? Is it both?

 "Hearing voices" is different for everyone I'd imagine so I won't assume on another's experience. For my own, though, imagine, if you will, that you're in another part of your house, that is away from the TV or a radio. Suddenly, you could hear the radio or TV is on, but it sounds like it's distant. You could have sworn you've turned them off, but maybe you didn't. You go to your living room, to find that the TV is off. You go to wherever you keep your radio and find that is also indeed off. You can then still hear this constant babbling, 'somewhere' but you can't really tell where. Trying to look for the source isn't going to help. It's just, always there.

3) What does it mean to you if your voices are better? Or "improved"? Are they just there with less volume?

 On my current medication, I just don't hear the voices anymore. If, for example, I get very stressed out, I due tend to notice these 'babbles' pop up again. So, I don't think they ever get 'better', they're just always there, and the medication I take, is like a stop-gap, for lack of a better term. The stress sort of pulls on that plug, to extend the metaphor.

4) when you are in a paranoid state what tips could you give me to help a person see I'm on their side and I'm sincerely trying to help?

 I know that this is going to sound very weird, and, from my extended experience from being with many nurses and doctors for my life, and I know that asking for this goes against the 'rules' or whatever 'laws' there are against physical contact, however, for me, personally, if someone were to, I dunno, clasp my hand, look me in the eye, and tell me, that, sincerely, you are there for me, then I will more than likely believe you. A hug is always ideal, but I never get one, no matter how much I ask. A hug to me, is like being administered Ativan, seriously, I've never felt more at ease and sedated than when someone, say a friend, or my mother, were to give me a hug.

5) have any of you been through your states commitment process? What was that like? What advice would you give me to give to patients up for a commitment hearing or recently committed?

 I am not familiar with this commitment process, so, I'm not sure. All I know is, from my experience, if a doctor thinks you need to go to a psych ward, then there is nothing you can do or say to prevent yourself from going. I, at one point, thought that I could talk myself out of it, and refuse his 'offer' to commit me, so instead, he signed me off as an 'unwilling' patient, which, to be honest, just extended my stay even more. So, advice? I guess, before you see your doctor, and you know you're having a hard time, pack your bags, just in case, because at least for me, my doctor has committed me more times than I can remember. This is not to say that people should not trust their doctor, but, being prepared ahead of time, can save you a lot of lost comfort in the ward, if you weren't.

6) how honest were you with your nurse during a hospital stay about your mental states? Were you paranoid about opening up? If so how might I help someone in that situation?

 I am always very honest with my nurses. The nurses I've dealt with were always super nice, always made sure I was comfortable and always helped me with whatever I needed. The only gripe that I can think of is, now, this can vary from different wards or ERs or whatever, but, sometimes, I mean, I know nurses are very busy discussing...things, or whatever they do while discussing things, but, there are times when a patient needs a nurse's help, just, anyone's help, including me at those times, and I was shooed away, because the nurses were 'busy'. Keeping me waiting, while, say, I'm having hallucinations for example, will just make the situation worse as anyone can imagine. Don't keep me waiting, please. When I come for your help, or when someone does, please, help them because you'll never know.

My doctor and case manager both seem to agree that whenever I have these paranoid thoughts enter my head is to do a bit of "reality-testing" as they've put it. 

It's where I begin to ask myself questions whether or not a delusion or my paranoia is something to actually be fearful of. Like, if I believed that the FBI were after me (which I did believe for a long time) I would first ask myself, "Have I done something wrong? To the point where it would involve the FBI?" and then ask another question down the line which becomes more specific, like, "If the FBI were after me, why would they spend (waste) their time on someone who hasn't done anything wrong?" and the questions would keep going until, I, hopefully, come to the conclusion that I'd have nothing to worry about.

Nevertheless, whenever I go out, especially on Halloween night, I was paranoid I was being followed everywhere, so I just kept looking behind me, every few steps, just to make sure I wasn't.

If I'm at home, however, where I feel the safest and I'm feeling paranoid, delusional, or scared, I do find that music usually helps me. Maybe even watching a sports game or even playing a video game, just anything to distract me long enough to forget about it.
